issues.legal_issue: Acquisition to enlarge a village site does not require the revenue authority to decide on enlargement before acquisition proceedings begin.
material_facts: Land was proposed to be acquired to extend a village site and house families left homeless by floods.
The challenger argued that the revenue authorities first had to establish that land within the existing village site was insufficient and decide to enlarge the site.
The applicable revenue provision addressed fixing and varying the limits of village sites, but did not make a prior enlargement decision a condition of acquisition.
issues.conclusion: The acquisition could proceed without a prior decision by the Collector, survey officer, or other revenue authority to enlarge the village site.
issues.legal_principle: Section 126 of the Bombay Land Revenue Code, 1879 concerns fixing and varying the limits of village, town, and city sites; neither that provision nor the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 requires a prior decision to enlarge a village site before acquisition for that purpose. The Court distinguished Chandrabhagabai Udhaorao v. Commissioner, Nagpur Division, Nagpur and Sitaram Maroti v. State of Maharashtra because those decisions concerned section 226 of the Madhya Pradesh Land Revenue Code, which expressly provided for prior findings about insufficiency and the availability of unoccupied land.

predicates.village_extension_acquisition: The proposed acquisition is for extending a village site.
predicates.governing_framework_lacks_prior_enlargem: The applicable legal framework does not condition acquisition for village extension on a prior decision to enlarge the village site.

issues.definition: When land is acquired to extend a village site and the governing framework imposes no prior-enlargement condition, the acquisition may proceed without a prior enlargement decision.

issues.legal_issue: A challenge to the suitability of land selected for acquisition fails absent a sufficient basis to interfere with the acquisition authority’s assessment, particularly when alleged alternatives are not properly identified.
material_facts: The land was proposed for acquisition to house families displaced by floods.
The challenger alleged that other land and open spaces were more suitable but did not provide proper particulars of those alternatives.
The acquisition authority’s assessment of the proposed land’s suitability was primarily for that authority to make, and no sufficient reason to interfere with its assessment was shown.
issues.conclusion: The Court declined to interfere with the acquisition authority’s assessment of the proposed land’s suitability, and the challenge based on alternative land failed.
issues.legal_principle: The assessment of the suitability of land proposed for acquisition is primarily for the Land Acquisition Officer. Interference is not warranted without a good reason, and a challenger who does not provide proper particulars of allegedly more suitable alternative land cannot establish a grievance that those alternatives were not considered.

rule.if: land_suitability_challenge and acquisition_officer_assessed_suitability and claimant_lacked_specific_alternative_land_details and no_basis_to_interfere

predicates.land_suitability_challenge: The proceeding challenges the suitability of land selected for acquisition.
predicates.acquisition_officer_assessed_suitability: The acquisition officer assessed the proposed land’s suitability for the stated public purpose.
predicates.claimant_lacked_specific_alternative_lan: The challenger did not properly identify the allegedly more suitable alternative land.
predicates.no_basis_to_interfere: No sufficient reason was shown to displace the acquisition officer’s assessment.

issues.definition: A land-suitability challenge fails when the acquisition officer assessed the proposed land, the challenger did not properly identify alternatives, and no sufficient reason supports interference.

issues.legal_issue: Delay caused by the challenger does not establish that the public purpose of an acquisition has ceased when there is no evidence that the purpose has been exhausted.
material_facts: The acquisition was intended to extend a village site for families displaced by floods.
The delay followed legal proceedings brought by the challenger and interim orders obtained by the challenger.
There was no evidence that the purpose of extending the village site had been exhausted; the Court noted that population growth could make the need for extension greater.
issues.conclusion: The challenger could not rely on the delay to establish that the public purpose no longer survived.
issues.legal_principle: A person cannot take advantage of delay caused by that person’s own legal proceedings and interim orders to claim that the public purpose has ceased. The claim also fails where there is no evidence that the stated purpose has exhausted itself.

predicates.public_purpose_survival_challenge: The proceeding challenges whether the public purpose of an acquisition remains in existence.
predicates.delay_caused_by_challenger: The delay in carrying out the acquisition resulted from legal proceedings or interim orders obtained by the challenger.
predicates.no_evidence_purpose_exhausted: There is no evidence that the stated public purpose has been exhausted.

issues.definition: When a challenger contests the continued existence of an acquisition’s public purpose, delay caused by that challenger does not establish that the purpose has ended if there is no evidence it was exhausted.

issues.legal_issue: A constitutional challenge to statutory provisions cannot be maintained after their validity has been upheld by the Supreme Court.
material_facts: The acquisition was challenged on the ground that the provisions governing preliminary notification and declaration of acquisition were unconstitutional.
The challenger conceded that the provisions’ validity could no longer be questioned because the Supreme Court had already upheld them.
issues.conclusion: The constitutional challenge did not survive and could not be maintained.
issues.legal_principle: The Court applied Manubhai Jehtalal Patel v. State of Gujarat, [1983] 4 SCC 553, in which the Supreme Court upheld the validity of the challenged provisions of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894.

predicates.constitutional_validity_challenge: The proceeding challenges the constitutional validity of statutory provisions.
predicates.controlling_supreme_court_precedent_uphe: An applicable Supreme Court decision has already upheld the validity of the challenged provisions.

issues.definition: A constitutional challenge to statutory provisions is rejected when an applicable Supreme Court decision has already upheld their validity.
